items.title: Prompt Injection Defense Patterns
items.abstract:
Prompt Injection Defense Patterns was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on measurement, benchmarking, red-teaming, and guardrails for deployed models. The project referenced by this session is NVIDIA/NeMo-Guardrails. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source NeMo-Guardrails project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Red-teaming is presented as a continuous program with ownership, triage, and regression tests rather than a one-off exercise.

The session distinguishes offline quality checks, online guardrails, and incident review, showing how each catches different failures.

Safety filters are evaluated on both false positives and false negatives, because over-blocking quietly destroys user trust and product metrics.

The speaker argues for reproducible evaluation artifacts: frozen datasets, versioned prompts, and recorded model snapshots.

Benchmark construction is described step by step: task sampling, rubric design, annotator agreement, and adversarial case mining.

The closing segment connects evaluation results to release decisions and rollback criteria.

Method and measurement. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. The speaker explains how they decided which optimizations were worth maintaining and which were removed after the experiment. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic.

Takeaways. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. The main takeaway is to measure the bottleneck before redesigning the architecture. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment.

Session context. The room was full, and the questions after the talk focused on deployment details rather than demos. The session is part of a longer track on building dependable model applications for internal and external users. Several audience members asked for reproducible configurations, and the speaker pointed to the referenced project as the starting point.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

items.title: Shipping Inference on Edge Devices
items.abstract:
Shipping Inference on Edge Devices was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on serving and optimizing large models under real production constraints. The project referenced by this session is mlc-ai/mlc-llm. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source mlc-llm project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

A detailed section covers cache reuse, prefix sharing, and eviction policies, with guidance on when the complexity of a shared cache pays for itself.

The session contrasts speculative decoding, lookahead decoding, and draft-model approaches, noting that acceptance rates are workload dependent.

The speaker frames serving as a scheduling problem: requests, KV cache blocks, batching windows, and hardware memory all compete for the same resources.

Benchmarks are reported at the request level, with percentile latency, throughput under saturation, and memory headroom so that operators can reproduce the result.

The speaker highlights easy wins first: better batching, fewer copies, tighter tokenizers, and honest load tests before investing in exotic kernels.

A final segment maps model size and context length to realistic single-node and multi-node deployment envelopes.

Method and measurement. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. The speaker explains how they decided which optimizations were worth maintaining and which were removed after the experiment. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The main takeaway is to measure the bottleneck before redesigning the architecture.

Memory services are evaluated on write amplification, retrieval precision, provenance, and the ability to delete user data safely.

Evaluation for retrieval is framed with recall at k, grounded answer rate, and citation quality, not only similarity scores.

The speaker demonstrates why embedding model changes require full reindexing and how to stage such migrations without breaking production.

The talk separates retrieval quality from memory quality: one is about finding evidence, the other about deciding what to keep and when to forget.

The talk demonstrates a local-first workflow where developers can replay a failing request with the exact model, prompt, and tool state that produced it.

The speaker highlights hidden operational costs: token accounting, noisy alerts, and experiments that never reach a clear conclusion.

Integration patterns are shown for CI pipelines that block releases when evaluation thresholds regress.

Prompt versioning is treated like code versioning, with review, rollback, and environment promotion rules that prevent accidental regressions.
